text: > Have you ever had to restore the exact state of things in an app, when you're manipulating and changing certain behavior of it, in a specific moment and a specific combination of values? And I can then resume from any past state/inspect any past state from the REPL, save any state, etc. I used to do it in the past with re-frame and events replayed but it was, IMO, a bit complicated for my needs. I now much prefer to have it all on the server-side and I simplified everything by using SSE / datastar (YMMV: for more complex needs, SSE may be insufficient). Everything is immutable/functional except for one atom that contains the app's state. And that one is basically both a DB and a DB of all previous states. I haven't done the full undo/redo as a tree yet (say like Emacs' undo/redo does) but it's been modeled to allow it. So I'll add that "navigation into past app state as a tree" (i.e. when I when backward then forked the state) visualization at some point. Immutability / functional code / determinism / the passage of time are all fascinating things to me. And once you've got the ability to walk through time as part of you language/REPL/app, testing and debugging becomes oh-so-much easier. P.S: and the LLM is surprisingly good at making sense of out how I modeled the passage of time and the ability to walk through time as part of the app.

text: > It’s not necessarily a natural monopoly. Having a private market does not make something not a natural monopoly. Healthcare, education, land, and energy are famously cases where market forces do not find a lowest possible price floor. the main things that cause a natural monopoly are things like high initial cost, a lower cost per unit created and the most important one a sub-additive cost function. If you have a single healthcare provider for example and 2 hospitals, you can have 1 IT team to handle both medical records, that is one engineering team, 1 database, 1 security team and then you have the costs that cannot be saved such as doctors nurses and staff in each hospital. Meanwhile if you have 2 healthcare providers you need 2 engineering teams, 2 dbs, and 2 cyber teams while the cost of doctors, nurses and staff remains untouched. That added cost makes the "competition" subadditive. You lose more than you gain by having multiple players in the market. Which is why American's spend more in healthcare than single payer systems like the ones in Europe. Just plain old boring math. And its not even a new concept. Adam Smith calls landlords "leeches" in his works

When people realized human-level intelligence is necessary to make natural language programming work, is basically when the idea died. Agreed, all IDs should be considered opaque. All user facing IDs should definitely be opaque and leak no information. I’m not a fan of UUIDv7, and don’t buy any of the arguments in favor of it. v4 is the better ID. My general preference though is 128 random bits encoded as base58 for user display. v4 isn’t even 128 random bits! Need creation time? Add a column. Need sequential ordering based on when rows were inserted? Add an auto increment column. “But my indexes” So what? Prove that it realistically impacts performance (spoiler alert, the rest of your app is likely far slower than the user facing ID lookups!) “But my foreign keys” Add a column. If you’re only in a single database server this can be the real primary key, likely an u32 or u64 if you truly need more than 4 billion rows. “But my hyper scale!” Then eat the cost of more servers for your distributed system. You can’t have your cake and eat it too.

text: GrapheneOS and AOSP are Linux distributions. Linux is not glibc, systemd, GNU coreutils, GCC and GNOME. text: I spent a couple years working at the platform (AndroidTV + Google Assistant) level on smart TVs. > any that want to do Alexa style voice prompts need it Not technically true. More modern smart TVs (~post-2021) put speech recognition models for the hotword only onto the DSP, and then have the DSP wake up the CPU for further auditory processing when it detects a hotword or remote button press. There are major power-efficiency benefits to this, because the DSP uses a fraction of a watt and can easily keep running while the TV is sleeping, while the CPU, Internet, and rest of the circuitry is a major power hog. Your smart TV or streaming dongle would basically never sleep if it were forever running the audio capture. For that matter, it's pretty rare for the device to actually run the speech recognition models on-device. Smart TV manufacturers are very sensitive to BOM costs, which means that their hardware is only powerful enough to run machine-learning models at the extreme high end of their product range. Most of the time the full audio gets streamed back to the Internet and the speech recognition & voice assistant gets run in the cloud, with commands streamed back to the TV. I won't say that it never has always-on audio listening; a significant number of devices I tested did. But I'll say this comes because they're poorly implemented. The DSP hotwording approach requires coordination between hardware and software developers, oftentimes across companies, and it's more complex to implement and a lot of executives don't care about the marginal consumer benefit it gives. Many smart TVs just guzzle power when they're off instead.

text: I’d just like to interject for a moment. What you’re referring to as “Android,” is in fact Android/Linux, or as I’ve recently taken to calling it, Android plus Linux kernel. Linux is not an operating system unto itself, but rather a kernel—a core component that manages hardware resources. Android uses the Linux kernel, but replaces the traditional GNU userland with its own runtime, libraries, and system framework. Many users run Linux-based systems every day without realizing it. Through a peculiar turn of events, the Linux kernel combined with Android’s userspace is often simply called “Android,” and many of its users are not aware that it is built on Linux at its core. There really is Linux in Android, and these people are using it, but it is just a part of the system they use. Linux is the kernel: the program in the system that allocates the machine’s resources to the other programs you run. The kernel is an essential part of the system, but useless by itself; it can only function in the context of a complete operating system. Android is normally used in combination with the Linux kernel: the whole system is basically Android/Linux, a Linux-based operating system with a distinct userspace, not a GNU/Linux system like traditional desktop distributions.

text: It's not just index pages. Generally databases write records into pages, which are then grouped into extents. If the primary key gives an ordering you can create new pages and start filling them up in an orderly fashion. If it's random, you are doing random inserts into pages everywhere all the time, then you start running out of room in pages and have to start splitting them. UUIDv7 solves the most painful parts of this problem in general and is a much better option for a Primary Key than UUIDv1-4.

text: I've used FreeDNS on occasion for test domain names, one-off experiments, and similar. I'm very appreciative this exists, but there are some pain points that similar services handle better. The domains are missing from the public suffix list. This impacts how cookies are handled by the domain names, with concerns the browser will allow software to set the cookie on the shared domain name instead of the subdomain. This can be a security problem. Getting added to the PSL may not happen: https://github.com/publicsuffix/list/pull/79 It can be difficult to get a free HTTPS certificate for your subdomain. Let's Encrypt applies per-domain name rate limits and these domain names see lots of issuance requests. There's a process to lift those limits, but last I checked FreeDNS didn't use it. You can still, of course, pay for a certificate. There's tons of abuse on free domains so you may find that your domain is blocked on various lists. Here are some compelling alternatives I use now, which manage these issues better: - https://messwithdns.net/ - Exceptionally well-made DNS console for learning DNS - https://open-domains.com/ - Uses Cloudflare, great Discord group - Even more: https://free.hrsn.dev/#/?id=domains

text: Many schemes do exactly this, if all you are doing is single table inserts that works pretty well. If you do anything that creates related records via foreign keys you start to run into lock contention. For example: If your insert requires a parent record with a single child record, you have to get the next sequential id which involves a non-preemptable single threaded lock, increment it, and send it back to the connection which requested it. In most databases this would mean writing the parent record and getting the sequential id of the parent record back so you can set the foreign key reference on the child record. Stored procedures are one way to mitigate the network transit time, but they don't solve the single threaded lock acquisition time. The reason most distributed systems use UUIDs or another flavor of distributed id is so you can generate the id for the parent record on the client, set the foreign key there as well, then send both records in as simple inserts. It's not that there aren't ways to work around it or mitigate it. Using a coordination free id, is just much easier to work with and scale in practice.
label: technical_explanation

text: No no, we don't want tokens. We don't want that at all. In the United States, users of Chase are already using FIDO2 to access their Chase accounts with hardware keys often priced at $15 or $20 made by a diverse set of 3rd party vendors such as Yubico, which has the same cryptography-grounded effects I suggested above. One hardware key can store private keys for several remote sites, this is a basic part of FIDO2. As far as holding onto hardware keys, users don't lose hardware keys/wallets when those are attached to a keychain and the users are instructed to attach to add it to their general car/house keys. Attached to general car/house keys/fobs, hardware keys survive user-chaos at a much better rate than smartphones do. Other security-focused IT pros/execs have reported the same. The key difference between those hardware tokens and hardware keys/wallets that do OpenPGP, or PIV, or the underlying cryptograpy functionality of "Bitcoin wallet", is they 1.] generate a cryptographic signature for the actual content ie "this much $xx.xx to meloney@example2.com" that the bank can keep and present later as reliable proof if appropriate and 2.] display on the screen the contents for #1, so a compromised user endpoint (smartphone or laptop) displaying false info is less likely to successfully bamboozle a user.

text: No, they are completely different. Determinism is the idea that if you have a perfect snapshot of the universe at one time, you could run that snapshot forwards or backwards using the laws of physics and have a complete history of the entire universe. It's a valid scientist idea, but Bell's Inequality experiments pretty much prove it false by showing that either realism or locality is false, and you kind of need both to have determinism. Meanwhile, superdeterminism is the idea that you can still have realism and locality by claiming that Bell's Inequality experiments are invalid because the universe could somehow "know" you are performing a Bell's Inequality experiment and rig it to get the "wrong" answer. Superdeterminism is equivalent to saying that we can't prove smoking causes lung cancer, because the universe might rig any science experiments to make it look like smoking causes cancer. Anytime you ask why the universe would do that or how you can prove anything in such a universe, they shrug their shoulders. It's a completely BS idea that got traction because specific people pushed it and others don't understand quantum physics enough to know how unserious of an idea it is.
label: technical_explanation
